doc_title: ApexConnect / ApexPharm Industrial Motor Fleet — Maintenance & Condition Monitoring Handbook v6.1
text:
CHAPTER 1 — FUNDAMENTALS OF CONDITION MONITORING FOR ROTATING MACHINERY

1.1 Why Condition-Based Maintenance (CBM) Replaces Preventive Maintenance
Traditional time-based preventive maintenance (PM) schedules replacement of components at fixed intervals regardless of actual condition. Statistical analysis of the Apex Conglomerate motor fleet (n=847 motors, 36-month observation period) demonstrates that time-based PM results in: 34% of replaced components still having greater than 60% of their useful life remaining (premature replacement, waste cost €1.2M/year); 18% of motors experiencing failure before the scheduled PM interval (unplanned downtime, cost €4.8M/year in lost production and emergency repair). Condition-Based Maintenance using real-time sensor data eliminates both failure modes by replacing components when condition indicators approach failure thresholds, not according to the calendar.

1.2 The P-F Interval: Foundation of Predictive Maintenance
The P-F curve describes the degradation trajectory of a component from initial potential failure (P) — when a defect first becomes detectable — to functional failure (F) — when the component can no longer perform its required function. The P-F interval (time between P and F) determines the earliest point at which maintenance can be planned. For rolling element bearings in Apex's motor fleet: vibration-based P-F interval averages 28 days (range: 7–90 days); temperature-based P-F interval averages 12 days (shorter because temperature rise is a late-stage indicator); acoustic emission P-F interval averages 45 days (earliest detectable signature). 

The practical implication for maintenance scheduling: vibration monitoring gives an average of 28 days to plan and execute bearing replacement before failure. Given Apex's maintenance lead time of typically 3–7 days to source parts and schedule downtime, vibration monitoring provides adequate margin in 94% of cases. Temperature monitoring alone is insufficient as the primary CBM method.

1.3 Sensor Architecture and Data Flow
Each motor in the Apex fleet (≥7.5 kW, operating >2,000 hours/year) is equipped with the following sensor suite: ICP accelerometer at drive-end bearing (ISO 13373-3 compliant mounting); ICP accelerometer at non-drive-end bearing; PT100 RTD winding temperature sensor; Hall-effect current transformer on phase L1; optional: acoustic emission sensor for high-criticality motors (>75 kW or serving critical processes).

Data is sampled at 1 kHz (time-waveform) and processed onsite by the edge gateway (Apex IoT Edge Node, firmware 3.4+) which computes: RMS velocity (0–1 kHz band, ISO 10816-3); Peak velocity; Crest Factor; kurtosis; Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) magnitude spectrum (0–500 Hz, 0.5 Hz resolution); one-third octave band spectra. Computed features, not raw waveforms, are transmitted every 6 hours to Elasticsearch (apex_operational_telemetry index) for storage, trending, and anomaly detection. Raw waveforms are stored locally on the edge node for 30 days and can be retrieved on-demand for detailed analysis.

CHAPTER 2 — BEARING FAILURE DIAGNOSIS AND FEATURE ENGINEERING

2.1 Rolling Element Bearing Defect Frequencies
Rolling element bearings generate characteristic defect frequencies when a surface defect (spall, pit, or crack) impacts the rolling elements or raceways during rotation. These frequencies are deterministic functions of bearing geometry and shaft speed, making them highly specific diagnostic signatures:

BPFO (Ball Pass Frequency, Outer Race):
BPFO = (n/2) × f_r × (1 - (d/D) × cos(α))
where n = number of rolling elements, f_r = shaft rotation frequency (Hz), d = ball diameter, D = pitch circle diameter, α = contact angle.

For the SKF 6312 bearing used in Apex standard motors (1450 RPM, n=8 balls):
BPFO = 8/2 × 24.17 × (1 - 0.414 × cos(0°)) = 3.59 × 24.17 = 86.8 Hz ≈ 87 Hz
This value (87 Hz) is the primary diagnostic frequency in the apex_operational_telemetry field fft_dominant_freq_hz when bearing outer race failure is in progress.

BPFI (Ball Pass Frequency, Inner Race):
BPFI = (n/2) × f_r × (1 + (d/D) × cos(α))
For the same bearing: BPFI = 3.59 × (1 + 0.414) × 24.17 = 122.5 Hz

BSF (Ball Spin Frequency): BSF = (D/2d) × f_r × (1 - (d/D)² × cos²(α)) = 45.3 Hz
FTF (Fundamental Train/Cage Frequency): FTF = f_r/2 × (1 - (d/D) × cos(α)) = 10.9 Hz

2.2 Feature Engineering for ML Models
The pre-computed fields in apex_operational_telemetry (fft_dominant_freq_hz, fft_harmonic_ratio) are derived features intended to give data scientists a head start. However, the most powerful features for bearing failure detection are:

Time-domain features:
- RMS velocity (vibration_mm_s): overall severity; ISO 10816-3 alarm at 4.5 mm/s for motors 15kW–75kW on rigid mounting
- Kurtosis: measures impulsiveness; healthy bearing ≈ 3.0; early bearing damage 5–10; severe damage >10; compute from raw waveform as E[x⁴]/(E[x²])²
- Crest Factor: Peak/RMS ratio; healthy ≈ 2.5–3.5; bearing damage >6.0
- High-frequency Energy Ratio (HFER): RMS in 2–10 kHz band / RMS in 10–1000 Hz band; detects early-stage subsurface fatigue before visible spectral peaks appear

Frequency-domain features:
- Spectral amplitude at BPFO and 2×BPFO: most specific indicator of outer race damage; use narrow-band RMS (±2 Hz around each frequency)
- Sideband energy around 1× RPM: indicates modulation due to shaft misalignment or rotor unbalance
- Harmonic Ratio: ratio of 2×RPM/1×RPM amplitude (fft_harmonic_ratio field); healthy ≈ 0.1–0.3; bearing damage >0.8 as harmonics proliferate

Trend features (require time-series from apex_operational_telemetry, filter by asset_id):
- Rate of change (ROC) of RMS over 7-day and 30-day windows: the acceleration of degradation is often more predictive than absolute level
- Residual variance: deviation from the seasonal/operational baseline (motor speed-corrected)

2.3 Model Architecture Recommendations
For Remaining Useful Life (RUL) regression:
Option A — Feature-based ML (recommended for hackathon): Extract the 8 features above from apex_operational_telemetry using a Pandas + Elasticsearch rolling window aggregation. Train XGBoost or LightGBM regressor on rul_days_true as target. Expected AUC-ROC on failure prediction (binary, threshold RUL<30d): 0.91–0.94. Training time: <30 seconds on 1,800 records.
Option B — Deep learning time series: LSTM or Transformer on raw time-series sequences per asset (60-day lookback). Requires careful handling of variable-length sequences and missing readings. Expected improvement over Option A: 3–8% AUC. Training time: 5–15 minutes on GPU.

CHAPTER 3 — MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES AND WORK ORDER INTEGRATION

3.1 Corrective Maintenance Workflow for Bearing Replacement
This procedure is triggered when the AFDS (Apex Failure Detection System) generates a MAINT-REQUIRED alert based on sensor data from apex_operational_telemetry. The complete workflow:

STEP 1 — Alert Receipt and Prioritization (Response: P1=4h, P2=24h, P3=72h):
Maintenance engineer receives alert via Apex CMMS (Computerized Maintenance Management System). Alert contains: asset_id, current RUL estimate, anomaly type, vibration trend chart (link to TECHDOC-FFT-* in apex_multimodal_assets), recommended action.

STEP 2 — Work Order Creation:
Open work order referencing: asset_id from apex_operational_telemetry; location (facility, cell); affected production line and estimated downtime impact; required spare parts (bearing model, quantity, from spare parts inventory); required skills (mechanical fitter, minimum Level 2 certification for motors >75kW).

STEP 3 — Pre-maintenance Preparation:
a) Isolation and lock-out/tag-out (LOTO) per ISO 50001: isolate all energy sources (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic); verify zero energy state with test equipment; apply personal lock and tag.
b) Retrieve work instructions from apex_unstructured_vault (search: "bearing replacement procedure" + asset_type) to ensure current revision is used.
c) Gather tools: bearing puller, hydraulic press or induction heater, torque wrench (calibrated ±4%), alignment laser, infrared thermometer, vibration analyzer for post-installation check.

STEP 4 — Bearing Removal and Inspection:
Record old bearing condition on maintenance report: type of damage (surface fatigue, adhesive wear, corrosion, electrical erosion, contamination); damage location (inner race, outer race, rolling elements, cage); estimated percentage of life consumed based on P-F curve analysis.

STEP 5 — New Bearing Installation:
Install new bearing per manufacturer instructions. For interference fit bearings: use induction heater to expand inner race to 80–100°C before fitting on shaft. Never use hammer blows (creates Brinell marks). Verify final clearance with feeler gauge. Grease per specification (SKF LGHB 2, 35g per bearing, purge excess via relief valve).

STEP 6 — Post-installation Verification:
Run motor at 50% load for 30 minutes before full-load operation. Take vibration reading with portable analyzer: compare to baseline spectrum in apex_multimodal_assets (TECHDOC-FFT-* for same asset or similar asset type). Acceptance criterion: RMS vibration <2.0 mm/s, no spectral peaks at BPFO/BPFI frequencies.

STEP 7 — Close Work Order and Update Elasticsearch:
Log all activities and measurements in CMMS. Update apex_operational_telemetry with maintenance event record (special document type: maintenance_event) linking to work order number. This record is used by the RUL model to reset the degradation baseline for the repaired asset.

doc_title: ApexConnect Network Infrastructure — Tower Maintenance and Performance Monitoring Manual v3.0
text:
CHAPTER 1 — TELCO TOWER MONITORING ARCHITECTURE

1.1 Overview of the ApexConnect Monitoring Framework
ApexConnect operates 847 base station towers across Central and Southern Europe. Each tower integrates radio access network (RAN) equipment monitoring with physical infrastructure monitoring (structural health, power systems, environmental) and feeds a unified data stream into the apex_operational_telemetry Elasticsearch index. This dual monitoring approach enables correlation between physical degradation of infrastructure and network performance KPIs — a correlation critical for root-cause analysis when customer complaints in apex_customer_interactions reference service outages.

The monitoring stack per tower site:
Physical Sensors: MEMS 3-axis accelerometer (structural vibration, mounted at 2/3 tower height); anemometer and inclinometer; cabinet temperature/humidity sensor; diesel generator load meter and fuel level sensor; door open/close security sensor.
RAN Performance Counters (polled every 15 minutes from eNB/gNB via SNMP/NETCONF): RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator, dBm); SINR (Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio, dB); PRB Utilization (Physical Resource Block utilization, %); Downlink Throughput; Uplink Throughput; Handover success rate; RACH (Random Access Channel) failures; Packet loss at backhaul interface.
Computed Fields in apex_operational_telemetry for telco assets: network_packet_loss_pct; signal_strength_dbm; all vibration and temperature fields shared with other asset types.

1.2 Failure Correlation: Physical Degradation → Network Impact
The following failure chains have been observed and validated in the Apex fleet, providing ground truth for training causal models:

Chain 1 — Power System Failure:
Generator fuel pump wear → fuel pressure drop → generator brownout → battery backup activation → reduced transmit power → RSSI degradation → packet loss increase → customer connection drops. Timeline: 6–18 hours from generator alert to customer impact. Detection: current_draw_amps spike on generator monitoring, followed 4–8h later by signal_strength_dbm degradation in apex_operational_telemetry.

Chain 2 — Antenna Tilt Drift (most common cause of gradual performance degradation):
Physical vibration from wind or traffic → antenna mounting bracket loosening → antenna tilt change → coverage pattern change → SINR degradation in affected cells → increased interference → PRB utilization increase (more retransmissions) → effective throughput drop. This is a slow-developing failure — detectable in vibration_mm_s trend data 30–60 days before significant SINR impact. The fft_harmonic_ratio field increases as mechanical looseness introduces sub-harmonic vibration.

Chain 3 — Backhaul Equipment Failure (as observed in ASSET-000042):
Microwave backhaul ODU (outdoor unit) overheating → transmit power reduction → packet loss on backhaul link → all RAN KPIs degrade (appears as if multiple simultaneous failures) → cell outage. Root cause: ODU cooling fan bearing failure (detectable via vibration_mm_s > 4.5 mm/s at high-frequency acoustic emission). In apex_operational_telemetry for ASSET-000042 (Tower FRA-12, Plant-Milano-A), the vibration signature at 87 Hz (BPFO frequency for the cooling fan bearing) was visible 23 days before complete failure — this data is present in the dataset for training failure prediction models.

text:
CHAPTER 2 — KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS AND ALARM THRESHOLDS

2.1 Network KPI Thresholds and Business Impact Mapping
Each KPI measured in apex_operational_telemetry for telco assets has defined thresholds that map to customer experience degradation levels:

Signal Strength (RSSI / signal_strength_dbm):
GREEN: > -90 dBm — Excellent coverage, full service
AMBER: -90 to -100 dBm — Acceptable for voice and basic data; streaming video quality reduced
RED: < -100 dBm — Poor coverage; voice calls may drop; data speeds below 1 Mbps
CRITICAL: < -110 dBm — No reliable service; customers unable to connect
Customer impact mapping (from cross-index analysis apex_customer_interactions + apex_operational_telemetry): For every 5 dBm drop below -95 dBm in a coverage zone, customer support tickets (intent: technical_support) increase by 23% in the 48h following the signal event. This correlation is the basis of the predictive customer impact model.

Packet Loss (network_packet_loss_pct):
GREEN: < 0.1% — No perceptible impact
AMBER: 0.1–1.0% — Slightly increased latency for interactive services; video buffering
RED: 1.0–5.0% — TCP performance degraded 30–60%; video streaming interrupted; VoIP quality issues (MOS < 3.0)
CRITICAL: > 5.0% — Severe service degradation; customers may experience "no service" perception even with signal present
Note: ASSET-000042 was measured at 18.7% packet loss at time of failure — this maps to the CRITICAL threshold and explains the high-severity customer complaints logged in apex_customer_interactions for the Milan-A service zone.

2.2 Predictive Maintenance Intervals for Telco Assets
Based on fleet failure statistics (847 towers, 7-year observation period):

Cooling fans (ODU, cabinet): MTBF 2.2 years; P-F interval 21 days; recommended CBM check: vibration reading every 30 days for fans >18 months old, every 14 days for fans >30 months old.
Tower structure (bolts, anchors): Corrosion-induced loosening: annual physical inspection mandatory per EN 50341; vibration anomaly detection (fft_harmonic_ratio > 1.5) triggers interim inspection within 7 days.
Battery backup systems: MTBF 4.5 years; monthly capacity test via automated battery test cycle; trend: internal resistance increase precedes capacity loss by 6–9 months.
Power amplifiers: MTBF 6.8 years; monitored via output power vs. input power efficiency ratio; efficiency drop > 8% from baseline triggers replacement planning.

2.3 Elasticsearch Query Patterns for Tower Diagnostics
For data scientists working with apex_operational_telemetry, the following query patterns are recommended for telco tower analysis:

Asset-specific time series retrieval:
GET apex_operational_telemetry/_search
{
  "query": {"bool": {"must": [
    {"term": {"asset_id": "ASSET-000042"}},
    {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": "now-90d"}}}
  ]}},
  "sort": [{"@timestamp": {"order": "asc"}}],
  "size": 500
}

Cross-asset anomaly detection (find all towers with packet loss > 5%):
GET apex_operational_telemetry/_search
{
  "query": {"range": {"network_packet_loss_pct": {"gt": 5.0}}},
  "aggs": {"by_asset": {"terms": {"field": "asset_id"}, "aggs": {"max_loss": {"max": {"field": "network_packet_loss_pct"}}}}}
}

Correlation query (customers in affected zone → check interaction complaints):
The join between apex_operational_telemetry (location: "Plant-Milano-A") and apex_customer_interactions (sentiment_score < -0.5) must be done at the application layer — Elasticsearch does not support native cross-index joins. Use the asset's location field as the grouping key and execute two sequential ES queries, joining results in application memory.

doc_title: ApexPharm Manufacturing — Process Engineering Guide for Solid Dose Production v5.3
text:
CHAPTER 1 — GRANULATION AND TABLET COMPRESSION PROCESS CONTROL

1.1 Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) and Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs)
In pharmaceutical solid dose manufacturing (tablets and capsules), Quality by Design (QbD) per ICH Q8(R2) requires identification of Critical Process Parameters (CPPs) — process inputs whose variation has a direct impact on product quality — and Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs) — output quality measures that must be within specification. For the ApexVital-200mg and ApexCardio-XR product lines:

CPP 1 — Granulation Endpoint (Wet Granulation Process):
Measured by: impeller torque (Nm), mixer motor current (A), particle size evolution via in-line NIR probe.
Target: Torque stable ±5% for 3 consecutive minutes; D50 particle size 180–220 μm at granulation endpoint.
Impact on CQAs: Under-granulation → poor tablet hardness, content uniformity failure; Over-granulation → dissolution failure (coating of API particles preventing drug release).
Field in apex_pharma_batches: chemical_parameters.particle_size_d50_um — spec limit 8–12 μm for final tablet (note: this is the final milled particle size, not granulation endpoint).

CPP 2 — Drying Temperature and Moisture Content:
Measured by: inlet/outlet air temperature (°C), Loss-on-Drying (LOD) every 20 minutes, NIR continuous moisture monitoring.
Target: LOD < 2.5% w/w at discharge; outlet temperature 45–55°C.
Impact on CQAs: Excess moisture → tablet capping, lamination, microbiological growth risk; Insufficient drying → dissolution failure, API degradation.
Field in apex_pharma_batches: chemical_parameters.moisture_content_pct — spec limit 0.5–3.2% w/w (see apex_pharma_batches.qc_status thresholds).

CPP 3 — Compression Force:
Measured by: main compression force (kN) via force sensor on tablet press; tablet hardness spot-check every 15 minutes.
Target: Main compression force 8–14 kN for ApexVital-200mg; hardness 80–120 N.
Impact on CQAs: Excessive compression → dissolution failure (over-compression), tablet sticking; Insufficient → friability failure, tablet breakage during coating.

1.2 Statistical Process Control (SPC) and Out-of-Specification Investigation
All CPPs and in-process controls are monitored in real-time on the Apex Process Analytical Technology (PAT) system, which feeds data to apex_pharma_batches at batch close. Western Electric SPC rules are applied automatically: Rule 1 (any single point beyond 3σ), Rule 2 (8 consecutive points same side of mean), Rule 3 (6 consecutive points trending in one direction), Rule 4 (14 points alternating up/down) — any rule violation triggers an automatic process alert and requires supervisor acknowledgment.

When a CQA result falls outside specification limits at final QC testing, the OOS investigation procedure (see POL sections in apex_unstructured_vault + apex_policy_vault) is initiated. Common root causes identified in the Apex fleet (database of 2,847 OOS investigations, 2019–2024): raw material variability (34% of OOS events) — supplier quality issue in incoming API or excipient; equipment calibration drift (22%) — force sensor, temperature sensor, or balance out of calibration; operator error (18%) — incorrect parameter entry, wrong raw material substituted; environmental excursion (14%) — temperature or humidity outside permitted operating range in manufacturing suite; unknown (12%) — no assignable cause found, batch classified as statistical outlier.

The 12% unknown rate represents a significant opportunity for ML-based root cause analysis. Features available in apex_pharma_batches for root cause prediction model: chemical_parameters (7 numerical features), facility (categorical, 3 values), production_date (seasonal effects), inspector_id (inter-analyst variability), supplier_id (supplier quality trends in apex_knowledge_graph). Target variable: qc_status (multi-class: RELEASED, HOLD, REJECT, QUARANTINE). Easter egg: correlating supplier_id with is_outlier rate reveals that SUPP-000003 has an outlier rate of 38% versus fleet average 12% — a supplier quality signal embedded in the data for DS teams to discover.
